findings.title: The arch-review-log row's central test claim is false at HEAD: the invocationCallOrder sort is NOT load-bearing, and no test kills its removal
findings.arbiter_reasoning: M4 replaced `[...single, ...set].sort((l, r) => l.order - r.order).flatMap(...)` with `[...single, ...set].flatMap(...)` in refusalCalls(). The whole unit file stayed green: 51 total, 0 failed. The mutation is semantically meaningful — refusalCalls() loses its chronological guarantee and returns arm order — and it is not equivalent: the two orders coincide only because every case that drives BOTH arms (the matrix test at :1443) runs the set-arm writer W4 LAST, so arm order happens to equal call order today. It is not on an unexecuted branch either: the mutated expression is evaluated by every one of the eight cases that call refusalCalls(). The row states the opposite as measured fact — 'sorts on `invocationCallOrder`, which is LOAD-BEARING and not tidiness' and 'Arm order mis-pairs every row the moment a second arm exists' — when a second arm exists NOW and arm order mis-pairs ZERO rows. The same false claim is repeated verbatim in the helper docblock at src/lib/solicitation/__tests__/ask-generation.test.ts:1246. The sort itself is correct and worth keeping; what is false is the claim that the suite protects it. Remedy: either reword the row and the docblock to say the sort is defensive and unexercised, or make it exercised — drive W4 before W1/W2/W3 in the matrix test (or add a case that interleaves the arms) so plain concatenation goes red.

findings.title: The new live-DB abort case does not kill the drift it was written for; three pre-existing cases already do
findings.reason: Arch-review-log claim (e) names one new hazard — 'the single statement drifting out of `sql.begin` on a later edit, where it would commit on its own connection' — and presents this case as the guard for it. M2b implements exactly that drift (`refusals` hoisted above the transaction, `await writeRefusalEvents(sql, refusals)` moved after `sql.begin`) and this case stays GREEN, because `sql.begin` rejects on the 22012 poison before the hoisted statement is reached. The mutant is caught, but by three pre-existing cases: :1682 'a refusal written by each render writer does not survive a later rollback of its outreach transaction' (whose settleGenerationExhaustion arm is behaviourally the same scenario, ~190 lines below), :1624, and :1391. The one mutant the new case does kill (M2, the pool handle in place of `tx`) is also killed by :1682. Remedy: either state in the row that the drift is covered by :1682 and this case is a real-Postgres-abort variant, or extend the case so a post-commit write is observable (assert the ledger rows on the SUCCESS path are visible only after the settlement commits, or drive the abort from inside the callback after the ledger write).

findings.title: Intake observability claim conflates the job's Sentry issue with the settlement's own failure signal
findings.reason: The claim is 'A CHECK violation still surfaces as a terminal generate_solicitation_asks settlement failure raised to Sentry by worker/job-failure-sink.ts.' `deadLetterWholeBatch` (worker/jobs/solicitation-batch/generate-failed-hook.ts:170-209) CATCHES the settlement throw, retries it in-hook, then logs a `terminal_settlement_*` status through `logFailureSafely` and returns; it never rethrows. job-failure-sink raises the ORIGINAL job failure whether or not the settlement succeeded, so Sentry cannot distinguish a settled batch from one whose settlement aborted on a CHECK violation. `docs/runbooks/beta-launch-alerting.md` carries no rule row for `terminal_settlement_abandoned` or its siblings. This path is PRE-EXISTING — the diff adds no new terminal or swallowed failure path — so it is recorded, not blocking.

findings.title: Fragile-assertion class: the 'no holes' case's title states a behavioural property, its assertions pin a structural one
findings.reason: The title is 'a generation exhaustion that finds no holes issues no Refusal write through either arm'. The assertions are `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` plus `mock.calls[0][1]` toEqual([]) — they require the call to HAPPEN. M6 (`if (refusals.length > 0) await writeRefusalEvents(tx, refusals)`) preserves the titled behaviour exactly (still no ledger write) and turns the case red. The pinning is deliberate per the case's own docblock (#1001's second-authority argument), so this is not a defect — but a reader debugging the red sees a title that says the opposite of what failed. Remedy: retitle to name the unconditional call, e.g. '... calls writeRefusalEvents unconditionally with an empty set and issues no ledger write'.
